archetypes.name: Plano-hyperbolic dielectric lens
archetypes.summary: Solid dielectric with a hyperbolic feed-side surface that turns a point source into a plane wave.

parameters.name: lens permittivity
parameters.description: 2.53 for Rexolite, 2.1 for PTFE, 11.7 for silicon

parameters.name: focal length
parameters.description: focus to lens vertex, on axis

parameters.name: rim angle
parameters.description: half-angle the lens subtends at the feed

parameters.name: illumination efficiency
parameters.description: Taper efficiency ALONE (it used to fold in spillover). DERIVED from the feed taper and the lens mapping; supply it to override.

parameters.name: feed taper at the rim
parameters.description: the feed pattern's own level at the rim angle, relative to its axis

parameters.name: spillover efficiency
parameters.description: feed power the lens intercepts. DERIVED; supply it to override

parameters.name: rim angle as a fraction of its limit, normalised

synthesis.notes: The hyperbolic surface in polar form from the focus: r(theta) = (n-1)F/(n*cos(theta)-1). Derived from equal optical path r + n*(z0 - r*cos(theta)) = F + n*(z0 - F), not quoted.

synthesis.expr: 2*(lens_nf + 1)*np.trapezoid((n_index - 1)*np.sin(np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001))*np.sqrt(np.cos(np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001))**lens_nf*(n_index - np.cos(np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001)))/(n_index*np.cos(np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001)) - 1)**3), np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001))**2/(((n_index - 1)*sin(rad(theta_rim_deg))/(n_index*cos(rad(theta_rim_deg)) - 1))**2*(1 - cos(rad(theta_rim_deg))**(lens_nf + 1)))
synthesis.notes: taper efficiency of the ray-mapped aperture field, integrated in the expression on 4001 points

analysis.notes: The surface is a hyperbola whose eccentricity equals the refractive index exactly - the geometric statement of Snell's law for this problem.

Beyond this the denominator n*cos(theta)-1 changes sign and the surface runs to infinity: rays at that angle cannot be collimated by this lens at all. A low-index lens is therefore forced to a long focal length.
Fresnel reflection at normal incidence, per surface. Silicon at n = 3.42 loses 30% per face, which is why high-index lenses need matching layers.
entry and exit, ignoring multiple internal reflections

From the Hankel transform of the ray-mapped aperture field, fitted over feed taper -20..-2 dB, the index and the rim angle up to 0.9 of its limit; within 0.2 lambda/D on the grid and 0.06 on points it never saw. Not a flat 70: a heavily tapered lens beam is far broader.
the aperture field at the rim relative to the centre: the feed taper plus the lens's own

validity: ray optics: the aperture must be many wavelengths across
theta_rim below max_rim_angle_deg, or the surface does not close
reflection loss assumes normal incidence at both faces; it is worse toward the rim, and multiple internal reflections are ignored
no dielectric absorption term - real lens materials add loss that grows with thickness and frequency
the flat face is untreated, so a real lens usually needs a matching layer or grooves

eta_ill, eta_spill, hpbw_deg and the edge illumination are geometric optics for a single refracting face and a cos^n feed; the rim angle must stay below 0.9 of its limit (acos(1/n) for a dielectric, acos(n) for metal plates) for the beamwidth fit

known_cases.source: Rexolite, n = 1.590597. The polar hyperbola r = (n-1)F/(n*cos(theta)-1) gives 135.168 mm at a 40 degree rim, so the aperture is 173.768 mm. Rays beyond 51.05 degrees cannot be collimated, since that is where n*cos(theta) = 1.
Fresnel at normal incidence: ((n-1)/(n+1))^2 = 0.0520 per face, so 0.8988 gets through both, costing 0.464 dB.
Silicon, n = 3.4205: 30.0% reflected at every face. Two faces cost 3.10 dB, which is why millimetre-wave silicon lenses are always matched.

n = 1.5906, rim 40 deg, -8 dB feed taper (cos^6.912): rays traced with Snell's law through the curved face (otahub.num.lens), power conserved along the traced ray tubes, beam by Hankel transform of that field - not the spec's closed-form mapping or its fit.

n = 3.4205, rim 40 deg, -8 dB feed taper (cos^6.912): rays traced with Snell's law through the curved face (otahub.num.lens), power conserved along the traced ray tubes, beam by Hankel transform of that field - not the spec's closed-form mapping or its fit.

n = 1.4491, rim 25 deg, -10 dB feed taper (cos^23.406): rays traced with Snell's law through the curved face (otahub.num.lens), power conserved along the traced ray tubes, beam by Hankel transform of that field - not the spec's closed-form mapping or its fit.

references: Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 9 (lens antennas)
Silver, Microwave Antenna Theory and Design, MIT Rad Lab vol. 12, Ch. 11
Surface equation derived here from the equal-optical-path condition
archetypes.notes: FROM THE FEED, THROUGH THE LENS. A ray leaving the focus at theta refracts at the curved face and crosses the flat face at rho(theta) = |n-1| F sin(theta)/|n cos(theta) - 1|; that mapping was checked by tracing rays with Snell's law at the actual surface (they leave parallel to 1e-9, and land where the formula says to 1e-15). Power conserved along ray tubes then turns a feed of pattern 2(n+1)cos^n into an aperture field, and the taper efficiency, spillover and beamwidth all follow. A HYPERBOLIC lens TAPERS the aperture on top of the feed: rim rays are spread over more aperture than axial ones, so -8 dB at the feed becomes -22.4 dB at the rim of the default Rexolite lens. Its feed should be broad - the best feed taper runs -6.7 to -9.3 dB over the cases checked - and a rim angle near the hyperbola's limit costs dearly: the default 40 degrees of a 51-degree limit peaks at 0.52 for taper x spillover, where 25 degrees reaches 0.73. The old flat 0.80 was nowhere near. The asserted eta_ill, which silently included spillover, is now the taper efficiency alone, beside a derived eta_spill.

archetypes.name: Luneburg lens
archetypes.summary: Sphere with a graded index that focuses a plane wave onto the opposite surface: any number of independent beams, no moving parts.

parameters.name: aperture efficiency
parameters.description: set by the feed's illumination of the sphere

parameters.name: normalised radius
parameters.description: where in the lens to report the index

analysis.notes: n(r) = sqrt(2 - (r/R)^2), so the core index is exactly sqrt(2) = 1.41421. That is the whole prescription: no free parameters, no design frequency.
Exactly 1 at the rim, which is why a Luneburg lens needs no matching layer - it is already matched to free space.
eps_r = n^2 = 2 at the core, falling to 1 at the surface
Exactly linear in r^2, which is convenient: stepped Luneburg lenses are built from concentric shells of constant permittivity spaced equally in r^2
the projected circle, not the sphere's surface
Exactly zero, by spherical symmetry: every feed position on the surface sees an identical lens, so beams scan to any angle with no degradation. No phased array can say that.

validity: ray optics: the diameter must be many wavelengths
the ideal lens is a continuous gradient; real ones are stepped shells, and the steps scatter - typically a few tenths of a dB and raised sidelobes
aperture efficiency is an input, set by how well the feed illuminates the sphere; a single feed rarely beats about 0.7
the lens is heavy and, in the stepped form, expensive to make - the reason it stays a niche solution despite its properties

known_cases.source: n(0) = sqrt(2 - 0) = 1.414214 exactly. The Luneburg prescription n(r) = sqrt(2 - (r/R)^2) has no adjustable constants.
n(R) = 1 exactly: the lens meets free space with no discontinuity, so there is nothing to reflect
A 300 mm lens at 30 GHz is 30.02 wavelengths across; at 0.65 aperture efficiency the gain is 37.61 dBi.
Spherical symmetry makes every scan angle identical. Expectation of zero, so an absolute tolerance.

references: Luneburg, Mathematical Theory of Optics, Brown University 1944
Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 9.7

archetypes.name: Fresnel zone plate
archetypes.summary: Flat plate of concentric zones that focuses by diffraction rather than refraction: cheap, thin, and inefficient.

parameters.name: phase quantisation levels
parameters.description: 1 = opaque (Soret) amplitude plate, 2 = half-wave phase reversal, 4 = quarter-wave stepped

synthesis.notes: Exact zone radius r_m = sqrt(m*lambda*F + (m*lambda/2)^2), from the condition that the path to the focus differs by m*lambda/2 between zone edges. The second term matters when F is only a few wavelengths.

analysis.expr: 1/pi**2 if phase_levels < 2 else (4/pi**2 if phase_levels < 4 else 8/pi**2)
analysis.notes: First-order diffraction efficiency. An opaque Soret plate blocks half the aperture and scatters most of the rest: 1/pi^2 = 10.1%. Reversing the phase instead of blocking it gives 4/pi^2 = 40.5%, and a four-level stepped plate 8/pi^2 = 81.1%. These are the standard binary and multilevel grating efficiencies.

analysis.expr: db10(1/pi**2 if phase_levels < 2 else (4/pi**2 if phase_levels < 4 else 8/pi**2))
db10((1/pi**2 if phase_levels < 2 else (4/pi**2 if phase_levels < 4 else 8/pi**2))*(pi*2*r_outer*f0/c)**2)

analysis.notes: the same aperture, perfectly illuminated
the beamwidth is set by the aperture, and is unaffected by the poor efficiency
The narrowest feature, and what sets the manufacturing tolerance. Zones get tighter outward, so a large plate is limited by the finest ring, not the biggest.
INDICATIVE. The zone radii are only correct at one frequency, and the focus blurs roughly as 1/M either side. A zone plate is a narrowband device.

validity: diffractive, so the design is correct at one frequency and degrades either side
efficiency figures are the standard first-order grating results, not full-wave computed - they ignore the finite thickness of a real phase plate and its shadowing at angle
higher diffraction orders carry the remaining power into spurious foci, and those are real stray-signal paths
the outermost zone width sets manufacturability and must stay comfortably above the etching or machining tolerance

known_cases.source: At 30 GHz (lambda = 9.993 mm) with F = 150 mm: r1 = sqrt(lambda*F + (lambda/2)^2) = 39.051 mm and r4 = 80.000 mm.
An opaque Soret plate reaches 1/pi^2 = 0.1013, a 9.94 dB penalty against a filled aperture.
Reversing the phase of alternate zones rather than blocking them gives 4/pi^2 = 0.4053 - four times the Soret plate, for the same outline.
Four phase levels reach 8/pi^2 = 0.8106, approaching a refractive lens

references: Hristov, Fresnel Zones in Wireless Links, Zone Plate Lenses and Antennas, Artech 2000
Born & Wolf, Principles of Optics, Ch. 8 (zone construction)
Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 9.6

archetypes.name: Metal-plate (constrained) lens
archetypes.summary: Stacked parallel plates whose guide index is below one, so the collimating surface is concave instead of convex.

parameters.name: plate spacing
parameters.description: must exceed 0.5 for the TE10 parallel-plate mode to propagate

parameters.name: illumination efficiency
parameters.description: Taper efficiency ALONE (it used to fold in spillover). DERIVED from the feed taper and the lens mapping; supply it to override.

parameters.name: feed taper at the rim
parameters.description: the feed pattern's own level at the rim angle, relative to its axis

parameters.name: spillover efficiency
parameters.description: feed power the lens intercepts. DERIVED; supply it to override

parameters.name: rim angle as a fraction of its limit, normalised

synthesis.notes: n = sqrt(1 - (lambda/2a)^2), the TE10 parallel-plate phase index. It is BELOW one, because the guided phase velocity exceeds c - the defining oddity of this lens.
Same equal-path construction as the dielectric lens, but with n < 1 the conic becomes an ELLIPSE rather than a hyperbola, and the lens is concave toward the feed.

synthesis.expr: 2*(lens_nf + 1)*np.trapezoid((1 - n_index)*np.sin(np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001))*np.sqrt(np.cos(np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001))**lens_nf*(np.cos(np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001)) - n_index)/(1 - n_index*np.cos(np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001)))**3), np.linspace(0, rad(theta_rim_deg), 4001))**2/(((1 - n_index)*sin(rad(theta_rim_deg))/(1 - n_index*cos(rad(theta_rim_deg))))**2*(1 - cos(rad(theta_rim_deg))**(lens_nf + 1)))
synthesis.notes: taper efficiency of the ray-mapped aperture field, integrated in the expression on 4001 points

analysis.notes: below 1, so the surface is an ellipse
the parallel-plate TE10 cutoff; below it nothing propagates between the plates

Thickness that adds one wavelength of differential path, so the lens can be stepped back by this much without changing the phase front. Zoning is what keeps a metal-plate lens thin, and it is also what makes it narrowband.
No dielectric reflection term: the plates are matched by flaring or by a matching section, not by Fresnel transmission

From the Hankel transform of the ray-mapped aperture field, fitted over feed taper -20..-2 dB, the index and the rim angle up to 0.9 of its limit; within 0.2 lambda/D on the grid and 0.06 on points it never saw. Not a flat 70: a heavily tapered lens beam is far broader.

dn per 1% frequency change. The index is strongly dispersive near cutoff, which is the metal-plate lens's real weakness: a few percent of bandwidth unless the plates are spaced well above cutoff, and that drives n toward 1 and the lens toward being flat and useless.
the aperture field at the rim relative to the centre: the feed taper plus the lens's own
beyond this the ellipse's aperture radius folds back and rays overlap

validity: plate spacing above lambda/2, strictly, or the guide is cut off
spacing below lambda keeps the next mode out
strongly dispersive: usable bandwidth is a few percent unquoted, and zoning makes it worse
ray optics, and the plate edges diffract - the model ignores both edge effects and the flare needed to match the plates to free space

eta_ill, eta_spill, hpbw_deg and the edge illumination are geometric optics for a single refracting face and a cos^n feed; the rim angle must stay below 0.9 of its limit (acos(1/n) for a dielectric, acos(n) for metal plates) for the beamwidth fit

known_cases.source: Plates 0.6 wavelengths apart at 10 GHz: 17.99 mm, cutoff 8.333 GHz, and n = sqrt(1 - (1/1.2)^2) = 0.552771 - well below unity.
The surface is an ellipse of eccentricity n = 0.5528, the mirror of the dielectric lens's hyperbola of eccentricity n > 1

n = 0.5528, rim 30 deg, -12 dB feed taper (cos^19.209): rays traced with Snell's law through the curved face (otahub.num.lens), power conserved along the traced ray tubes, beam by Hankel transform of that field - not the spec's closed-form mapping or its fit.

n = 0.5528, rim 45 deg, -14 dB feed taper (cos^9.301): rays traced with Snell's law through the curved face (otahub.num.lens), power conserved along the traced ray tubes, beam by Hankel transform of that field - not the spec's closed-form mapping or its fit.

n = 0.7806, rim 20 deg, -10 dB feed taper (cos^37.018): rays traced with Snell's law through the curved face (otahub.num.lens), power conserved along the traced ray tubes, beam by Hankel transform of that field - not the spec's closed-form mapping or its fit.

references: Silver, Microwave Antenna Theory and Design, MIT Rad Lab vol. 12, Ch. 11
Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 9.4
archetypes.notes: FROM THE FEED, THROUGH THE LENS. A ray leaving the focus at theta refracts at the curved face and crosses the flat face at rho(theta) = |n-1| F sin(theta)/|n cos(theta) - 1|; that mapping was checked by tracing rays with Snell's law at the actual surface (they leave parallel to 1e-9, and land where the formula says to 1e-15). Power conserved along ray tubes then turns a feed of pattern 2(n+1)cos^n into an aperture field, and the taper efficiency, spillover and beamwidth all follow. A METAL-PLATE lens (n < 1, an elliptical face) does the opposite: it BRIGHTENS the rim, so -12 dB at the feed is -8.5 dB at the rim of the default design. Its feed should be narrower than a dish's - the best runs -11.8 to -13.6 dB - and taper x spillover reaches 0.89-0.95, where the old flat 0.75 undersold it. The ellipse also has a limit the spec did not state: the aperture radius peaks at cos(theta) = n and folds back beyond it, so the rim angle must stay below acos(n). The asserted eta_ill, which silently included spillover, is now the taper efficiency alone, beside a derived eta_spill.
